clue.text: Torture working for an eastern newspaper in 5 Across story

parts.note: 'it was sheer hell' means it was torture, agony; the colloquial word wanted is the one for killing
a machine that is on is working
a plausible masthead for a paper from the East: the Orient is the East

explanation.surface: A lurid tale of torture carried out on behalf of some newspaper in the Far East.
explanation.walkthrough: The last chunk is an invented newspaper title, The Orient Express, rather than a synonym chain; 5 Across is CHRISTIE, so the definition asks for one of her books.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's 1934 Poirot novel set aboard the famous luxury train is among her best-known detective mysteries.

clue.text: Blue Berets relished investing northern plain

parts.note: United Nations peacekeepers wear blue berets

indicators.note: to invest is to clothe or surround, so one piece is wrapped around another

parts.note: relished means loved, enjoyed greatly
N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: UN peacekeepers enjoying something they have put money into in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue Berets' reads as a description of headgear, but it stands for the UN, whose peacekeeping troops wear them; the abbreviation N then sits inside the word for relished.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without decoration or ornament is simple and bare, which is what plain means here.

clue.text: Clown is so dejected

parts.note: surface reading: the sad clown, cheerful outside and miserable within; setter's reading: look at the word itself, whose middle three letters spell a word meaning down

explanation.surface: The old image of the sad clown, merry for the audience but gloomy at heart.
explanation.walkthrough: C-LOW-N has LOW at its heart, and low means down, so the word Clown is literally 'down-hearted'; the answer then also means dejected.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling low in spirits, discouraged and gloomy, is the plain meaning of the compound adjective.

clue.text: Camilla perhaps put up by Republican circle

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican
the letter O is circle-shaped

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: to put something down is to lay it

explanation.surface: Queen Camilla being hosted by a group of anti-monarchists, an unlikely social occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' looks like accommodating a guest; here it is a word for put, flipped. 'By' just places it beside the other two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Camilla is a member of the British monarchy, so she is one example of a member of a ruling family.

clue.text: Writer excluding Mike from this crime novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters take a new form
excluding means leaving out, so a letter is removed before rearranging

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written

explanation.surface: An author removes a character called Mike from a detective story she is writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crime novel' looks like a genre, but 'novel' is the anagram signal; remove M from THIS CRIME and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie was the English novelist famed for Poirot and Miss Marple detective stories.

clue.text: Liquor Charlie stored in back-to-back houses

indicators.note: two things back to back face opposite ways, so the second copy runs backwards
something stored in a place is kept inside it

parts.note: HO is the abbreviation for house, and there are two of them
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone called Charlie hiding booze in a row of back-to-back terraced houses.
explanation.walkthrough: Back-to-back houses are a kind of British terraced housing, but here they mean HO followed by HO reversed, giving HOOH with C tucked inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Hooch is slang for strong or illicitly made alcoholic spirits, the cheap stuff of bootleggers.

clue.text: National flag seen over hospital

definitions.note: the clue's noun means a citizen; the answer is an adjective or a plural noun for the people

parts.note: the yellow iris is also called a flag
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: A country's flag flying above a hospital building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'National flag' looks like one phrase; split it, so that National is the definition and flag is the plant. In a down clue, over means placed above.
explanation.definitionFit: A national is a citizen of a particular country, and someone from Ireland belongs to that nationality.

clue.text: Port, one from Anatolia, Mitford-approved?

parts.note: Anatolia is the Asian part of Turkey
Nancy Mitford popularised U (upper-class) versus non-U usage

explanation.surface: A port-drinking Turk whose manners pass muster with the snobbish Mitford sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: Port looks like the drink; it is a harbour city. U means upper-class, the label Nancy Mitford's essay made famous for posh English usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Turku is a historic harbour city on the southwest coast of Finland, the country's former capital.

clue.text: Nuisance lowering head before a German artist

indicators.note: bringing the top letter down a place rearranges the word's order

parts.note: a pest is a nuisance
EIN is German for a or one

explanation.surface: An irritating person bowing their head in front of a German painter.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letter of PEST drops one place to become second, giving EPST; 'a German' is the German word for a.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Jacob Epstein was the American-born British sculptor known for bold modernist bronzes and carvings.

clue.text: Golf consistently snubbed in 7 Down county

indicators.note: snub originally meant to cut short, so the word loses its tail

parts.note: Golf is G in the NATO phonetic alphabet
something done consistently is done always

explanation.surface: Golfers repeatedly cold-shouldered somewhere in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snubbed' sounds social; here it means docked, losing its final letter. 7 Down is IRISH, so the definition is an Irish county.
explanation.definitionFit: Galway is a county on Ireland's west coast, with a city of the same name.

clue.text: Stabs brawling Paris don

indicators.note: brawlers tumble about in disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A university lecturer from Paris gets into a knife fight.
explanation.walkthrough: Stabs reads as a noun at first, but it is a verb here, matching the answer used as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A poniard is a slim dagger, and as a verb it means to pierce someone with such a weapon.

clue.text: Eliot tortured with thoughts about her unfinished work

indicators.note: tortured means twisted out of shape, so the combined letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: unfinished means the word her stops short of its final letter

parts.note: taken as written, before its last letter goes

explanation.surface: A critic says George Eliot agonised over a book she never finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' cuts HER to HE; 'tortured' then scrambles ELIOT, THOUGHTS and HE together. The answer is Virginia Woolf's novel, not Eliot's, so the author named is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the title of a 1927 novel by Virginia Woolf, so it is a literary work.

clue.text: Gates repaired by officer in shape

indicators.note: a repaired thing has been taken apart and put back together, here in a different order

parts.note: taken as written
LT is the abbreviation for lieutenant

explanation.surface: Broken gates fixed up by a military officer and now in good condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In shape' looks like 'in good condition'; 'in' is only a link and shape is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Gestalt, borrowed from German psychology, means an organised whole form or configuration perceived as more than its parts.

clue.text: Monkey caught in Florida location

indicators.note: to catch what someone says is to hear it, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: to monkey with something is to tamper with it; in a non-rhotic British accent the final -er sounds like -a

explanation.surface: A primate on the loose is finally captured somewhere in Florida.
explanation.walkthrough: Monkey looks like an animal, but it is the verb meaning to meddle. The sound match relies on British speech, which drops the final R.
explanation.definitionFit: Tampa is a large city on Florida's Gulf Coast, on Tampa Bay.

clue.text: See 1
Attackers wearing Red Baron's wellies?

parts.note: to be dressed in something is to be wearing it

indicators.note: the Red Baron was a German flying ace, so the word is said in a German accent

parts.note: wellies are rubber boots, like waders; said by a German speaker, the W comes out as V

explanation.surface: Picturing the famous German fighter pilot in rubber boots, a comic image of the Great War.
explanation.walkthrough: Wellies (wellington boots) are rubber boots, and waders are high waterproof boots; in a stage German accent W becomes V.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who enter a territory by force to conquer it are aggressors launching an assault.

clue.text: Start out from London suburb — or edge towards one?

indicators.note: with its start gone out, the word loses its first letter

parts.note: Hendon is a suburb in north London

explanation.surface: Setting off from a London suburb, or perhaps sidling towards one.
explanation.walkthrough: Hendon is a north London suburb. The question mark warns that the definition is playful: approaching something with an edge leading.
explanation.definitionFit: Positioned with the narrow end facing something, as a ship or plank presented end-first rather than broadside.

clue.text: Potentially chewy meat from dog leg

parts.note: a mutt is a mongrel dog
in cricket the leg side is also called the on side

explanation.surface: Tough meat that turns out to come from a dog's leg, a butcher's scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: Leg is the cricket field: the leg side and the on side are the same half of the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat from a mature sheep is tougher than lamb, so it can be chewy if not slow-cooked.

clue.text: See 23
Checked return of French marine force

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: DE is French for of
the tide is the force that moves the sea

explanation.surface: Monitoring the comeback of a French navy unit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marine force' suggests a body of sailors, but it is the tide; 'of French' gives DE, and the whole string is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Text that has been checked has been reviewed and corrected for publication.

clue.text: See 1
In the morning don't drink ordinary liqueur

parts.note: AM is the abbreviation for morning
'are TT' means are teetotal, TT being the abbreviation for teetotal
O is the abbreviation for ordinary

explanation.surface: Advice to skip ordinary booze before noon, ironically ending in a sweet Italian drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don't drink' reads as an order; it is the statement 'are TT', where TT means teetotal.
explanation.definitionFit: Amaretto is a sweet almond-flavoured Italian digestif.

clue.text: Maybe verbiage not recalled by immature Nick

parts.note: padding is wordy filler, and verbiage is an example

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
green means unripe or inexperienced

explanation.surface: Childish Nick produces long-winded waffle that nobody can remember.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick looks like a man's name; it is British slang for a police station. This high-security London station closed in 2018.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick is British slang for a police station, and this famous central-London one held terror suspects.

clue.text: 5 Across story headline not deciphered with penetrating article

indicators.note: something penetrating goes inside, so one piece enters the other
deciphering untangles a code, so the letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the definite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper story whose cryptic headline nobody could decode, with an article pushing into it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Headline' and 'article' suggest journalism; the first is anagram material and the second is THE, which pushes into the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's 1937 Poirot mystery is set aboard a Nile steamer in Egypt.

clue.text: Some Angevin troops opening passage

indicators.note: some means a portion, so the letters are a run inside the words that follow

parts.note: the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Medieval soldiers from Anjou forcing their way through a narrow pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening passage' sounds military, troops forcing a way through, but it means the start of a piece of music or writing.
explanation.definitionFit: An introduction to a song or text is the first section, abbreviated informally.

clue.text: Changing direction in wood makes hand warmer

indicators.note: changing direction swaps one direction for another, right for left, within the word for a wood

parts.note: a grove is a small wood

explanation.surface: A woodworker changes the grain direction and fashions something to warm the hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing direction in' turns the R (right) in GROVE into an L (left), both standard direction abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: A glove is worn over the hand, chiefly to keep it warm, so it is a hand warmer by description.

clue.text: Man-at-arms called out in darkness

indicators.note: something called out is spoken, so it counts by its sound

parts.note: a knight is a mounted man-at-arms; the K is silent

explanation.surface: A soldier shouting into the dark.
explanation.walkthrough: The K at the start of the soldier's word is silent, so the two words sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: The hours between dusk and dawn are the period of darkness.

clue.text: Old suit — pressing demands made?

parts.note: an ex is a former thing or partner
a lawsuit is a legal action

explanation.surface: A worn-out suit that badly needs an iron, or a lawsuit pressed hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old suit' and 'pressing' suggest clothes and ironing; suit is a lawsuit and pressing means insisting.
explanation.definitionFit: An exaction is the forcible demanding of payment or service, as by an oppressive ruler or tax collector.

clue.text: Green part in smoke that rolls over tongue

indicators.note: turned over means flipped end to end, so the letters run backwards
to take part in is to be inside something, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a smoke you roll is a cigarette, informally a cig
a lea is a grassy meadow, a green

explanation.surface: Someone taking a drag of a green-tinged roll-up and savouring it on the tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: Green looks like an adjective, but it is a noun for a meadow; that goes inside the short word for a cigarette, and the whole is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaelic is the Celtic language of Ireland and Scotland, and a tongue is a language.

clue.text: Vessel from Switzerland coming in earlier

indicators.note: something coming in enters, so it sits inside another piece

parts.note: sooner means earlier
CH is the international code for Switzerland

explanation.surface: A ship arriving from Switzerland ahead of schedule, odd for a landlocked country.
explanation.walkthrough: CH stands for Confoederatio Helvetica, Switzerland's Latin name, used on car stickers and web addresses.
explanation.definitionFit: A schooner is a sailing ship with two or more masts; it is also a tall glass for sherry or beer.

clue.text: Maybe like Red Baron flier showed the way

parts.note: a tit is a small bird
to lead is to show the way

explanation.surface: The Red Baron, the flying ace, leading his squadron into combat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' points at the German pilot, but here it is just a small bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Manfred von Richthofen held the rank of baron, a noble rank, so he had an aristocratic rank.
